passages.happening:
The chapter opens on the other side. When the kings of the land hear that the LORD dried up the Jordan in front of Israel, ‘their hearts melted and their spirits failed for fear of the Israelites’ (verse 1).

Israel does not attack. God gives Joshua a different order: “Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel once again” (verse 2).

The writer explains why. The men who came out of Egypt had been circumcised. They had all died in the wilderness, because they did not obey the LORD. Their sons, born on the way, had never been circumcised (verses 4-7). So Joshua circumcises them now, and the whole camp stays where it is until the men are healed (verse 8).

Then God speaks: “Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you.” The place is called Gilgal from then on (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Circumcision was the sign of the covenant God made with Abraham. Every male in Abraham's family was to carry it in his body, as a mark that this people belonged to the LORD. Other peoples of the ancient world practiced circumcision, the Egyptians among them. Israel gave it this meaning.

The sign had lapsed during the forty years in the desert. The text does not say why. Readers have suggested the hardships of travel, or the broken standing of the generation that had refused to enter the land. Whatever the reason, the people who have just crossed the river do not carry the mark of the promise they have come to receive.

Flint knives were stone knives. They went on being used for this rite long after metal tools were common.

A commander would call the timing foolish. Israel has just entered enemy country. The kings of the land are frightened and off balance. And at that moment every fighting man in the camp is made unable to fight for days. An old story in Genesis shows how exposed men are in that condition. Israel is safe only because God keeps it safe. Before the people are allowed to take anything, they are made to belong and made to depend.

The order of events says something too. God brought Israel across the river first, by a miracle, and asked for the sign afterward. The covenant mark is not the price of entry. It is the answer of a people who have already been carried over.

‘The reproach of Egypt’ has been understood in several ways. It may be the shame of having been slaves. It may be the mockery the Egyptians would have made if Israel had died in the desert. It may be the disgrace of the unbelieving generation and its uncircumcised sons. The text does not choose, and all three belong to the same story. Whatever the shame was, God says it is gone.

The name Gilgal sounds like the Hebrew verb that means ‘to roll’. Place names in the Old Testament often carry a memory in this way.
passages.later:
The sign was first given to Abraham: “You are to circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and this will be a sign of the covenant between Me and you” (Genesis 17:11).

Moses had already said that the outward sign pointed to something inward that only God could do: “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live” (Deuteronomy 30:6).

Paul takes up that thought: ‘circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code’ (Romans 2:29).
passages.asks: God stopped an army on the edge of its first battle so that the people could be marked as his. Ask what you are hurrying past in order to get on with the work. And hear what God said at Gilgal: the reproach is rolled away. Ask what old shame you still carry as if it had the last word about you, and who told you it did.

passages.t: Passover in the land, and the last of the manna
passages.happening:
“On the evening of the fourteenth day of the month, while the Israelites were camped at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho, they kept the Passover” (verse 10).

The next day they eat food grown in Canaan for the first time: ‘unleavened bread and roasted grain from the produce of the land’ (verse 11).

“And the day after they had eaten from the produce of the land, the manna ceased. There was no more manna for the Israelites, so that year they began to eat the crops of the land of Canaan” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The Passover is the meal that remembers the night God brought Israel out of Egypt. It was kept on the fourteenth day of the first month. Israel left Egypt on a Passover and enters its new life in the land on a Passover. The forty years between are closed like a bracket.

The order of the chapter is not an accident. The law said that no uncircumcised man could eat the Passover. The men had to receive the covenant sign before they could sit down to the covenant meal. That is why the knives come before the lamb.

Roasted grain was fresh barley from the spring harvest, the first crop of the year in the Jordan valley, toasted over a fire. It was ordinary food. After forty years of manna it must have tasted like arrival.

Manna was the bread God gave Israel in the wilderness. It fell six mornings out of seven for forty years. No one under forty in that camp had known a day without it. Then one morning there was none.

The writer tells this without sadness, and a reader should notice why. The manna did not stop because God had stopped providing. It stopped because he was now providing in another way, through soil, rain and harvest. The miracle gave way to the ordinary gift, and both came from the same hand. Moses had warned that this would be the harder test. A people fed by fields would be tempted to forget who fed them.
passages.later:
Exodus had already told readers when the manna would end: “The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land where they could settle; they ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan” (Exodus 16:35).

Moses said what the manna had been for: ‘so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD’ (Deuteronomy 8:3).

Jesus spoke of manna when a crowd asked him for a sign, and pointed past it to himself: “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst” (John 6:35). And Paul wrote, “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).
passages.asks: The manna stopped the day the harvest began. Ask whether there was a time when God's care for you was plain and unusual, and whether you have taken its ending to mean that he stopped caring. Then look at your ordinary bread: your work, your wages, the food on the table. Ask whether you receive it as a gift or as something you produced.

passages.t: The commander of the LORD's army
passages.happening:
Joshua is near Jericho. He looks up and sees a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword in his hand.

Joshua walks up to him and asks, “Are You for us or for our enemies?” (verse 13).

The answer begins with one word: “Neither.” Then the man says who he is: “I have now come as Commander of the LORD’s army” (verse 14).

Joshua falls with his face to the ground and asks, “What does my Lord have to say to His servant?” (verse 14).

The commander gives one order. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.” And Joshua did so (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Joshua's question is the question of a soldier, and it is a reasonable one. A stranger with a drawn sword near an enemy city is either a friend or a threat. In Joshua's mind there are two sides.

The answer refuses the question. The man is not on Israel's side and not on Jericho's. He has come at the head of another army altogether. ‘The LORD's army’ is most likely the host of heaven, the angels who serve God. The Hebrew word for ‘commander’ is used in the book of Daniel for heavenly princes.

A reader who has followed the book this far might have expected a different answer. God has promised to be with Joshua. He has stopped a river for Israel. Surely he is ‘for us’. The commander's one word guards against a mistake that armies and nations have made in every age. God had bound himself to Israel by promise. But God does not join anyone's side as a follower. He is not a weapon that Israel owns. Two chapters from now Israel will be defeated because of sin in its own camp, and the lesson of this meeting will be learned in blood. The question Joshua needed to ask was not whose side God was on. It was whether Joshua was on God's.

Joshua understands at once. He stops asking about sides and asks for orders. He calls himself ‘servant’. The general of Israel's army lies face down in front of his own commander.

The order he receives is not a battle plan. It is the order God gave Moses at the burning bush, almost word for word: take off your sandals, because this ground is holy. To remove one's sandals was a sign of reverence. The ground is in enemy country, near the walls of a Canaanite city. It is holy because of who is standing on it.

So the last thing that happens before the battle of Jericho is that Joshua worships. The book places this scene here on purpose. Everything in the next chapter, the marching, the horns, the silence, is to be read as an act of obedience to this commander.
passages.later:
When God first called Moses, he said, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5).

Another man once met the same sight on a road: “Then the LORD opened Balaam’s eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand. And Balaam bowed low and fell facedown” (Numbers 22:31).

Centuries later the prophet Elisha's servant was shown the army Joshua was told of: ‘he saw that the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha’ (2 Kings 6:17).
passages.hard:
Who is the commander of the LORD's army?

The text does not name him, and readers have held three main views.

Many early Christian writers, and many since, have taken him to be the Son of God appearing before he became man. They note that he receives Joshua's reverence and calls the ground holy, as God did at the burning bush.

Others identify him as the angel of the LORD. In several Old Testament passages this figure speaks as God himself, and how he is related to God is left open.

Others take him to be a created angel of high rank, perhaps Michael, whom the book of Daniel calls a great prince. On this view Joshua's bowing is a mark of deep respect, and the ground is holy because God is present and not because of the messenger.

The scene breaks off with no battle plan, and the next chapter continues with the LORD speaking to Joshua directly. Some take that as a sign that the commander and the LORD are closely identified. These notes do not choose among the views.

What is not in dispute is the meaning of ‘Neither’. The LORD's army does not belong to Israel. Israel is called to belong to the LORD. No people, church, party or nation since has had the right to assume that God is on its side, and this verse stands against every attempt to enlist him.
passages.asks: Joshua asked, ‘Are You for us or for our enemies?’ and was told, ‘Neither.’ Ask where you have assumed that God is on your side: in a quarrel, in your politics, in a conflict at church or at home. Ask what would change if your first question were whether you are on his. Then do what Joshua did next. Ask him, ‘What does my Lord have to say to His servant?’
